title: Why Three-Year Degrees Are Gaining Spotlight in the U.S.
subtitle: Shortened programs promise time and money savings, yet face criticism
excerpt: Three-year degrees are on the rise in the U.S., offering shorter courses and lower costs, though concerns about quality and recognition persist.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The growing demand for three-year degrees in the United States stems from the need to balance work, family, and study, as well as the high cost of traditional four-year programs. The proposal to reduce the credit load to about 90 credits has attracted students looking to enter the workforce more quickly.

How Three-Year Programs Work

These courses condense traditional content, eliminating electives and shortening semesters to five‑to‑ten‑week periods. Upon completing 90 credits, the student earns the same bachelor’s title as a 120-credit program, but a year earlier.

Who Is Adopting This Format

Students such as 34‑year‑old Giles Sims chose a Bachelor of Applied Communication at Ensign College to avoid being out of the job market for four years. Another example is Jill Cohen, who is finishing a teaching degree in an accelerated program at Indiana Wesleyan while working at a school.

Perceived Advantages for Advocates

Proponents point out that reduced time and costs help mitigate the accessibility crisis in higher education. RAND reports that 26 states already have at least one institution offering these programs, totaling 119 options announced by May.

Criticisms and Concerns

Organizations such as the American Association of University Professors question whether the credit reduction could devalue the degree. Todd Wolfson, president of the AAUP, describes the measure as “cutting corners.” Additionally, doubts remain about the acceptance of these diplomas in graduate programs and careers that require state licenses.

Future Impact on the Educational Landscape

Although there are still no consolidated standards for admitting three‑year graduates into advanced courses, the expansion of these programs could pressure other institutions to rethink their curriculum structures. Meanwhile, students continue to weigh whether the time and money savings outweigh potential recognition limitations.

With information from ONE Championship, AP News.
